name: Sidney Mavor
bio: 'The only other individual of decent family and upbringing besides Shelley' among the Crown's young men (Hyde): living at 66 St Helen's Gardens, North Kensington, and by 1895 in partnership in a City business. Taylor met him at the Gaiety Theatre in 1892, groomed him for the Kettner's dinner given by Schwabe ('Mr. Wilde likes nice clean boys'), and Wilde sent him a silver cigarette case inscribed 'Sidney from O. W., October, 1892' before an overnight at the Albemarle Hotel. On the stand he repeated his Bow Street denial — no misconduct, no impropriety ever — and the Mavor counts were struck out; Hyde's footnote preserves Douglas's own account of coaching that denial in the Bow Street corridor. Atkins had 'heard him called Jenny Mavor.'
bio_sources: Hyde, Trials (1948), Introduction pp. 72-73 with n (counts struck out; the corridor story from Douglas's Autobiography, 2nd edn. p. 119) and pp. 85-86 (Mavor dropped at the final trial)
Atkins's testimony ('Jenny Mavor'), Hyde, Trials (1948), p. 207
Ellen Grant's testimony ('Mavor and Mason stayed there for nights with Taylor'), Hyde, Trials (1948), p. 199
bio_note: No birth/death dates found; the General Index of Complete Letters (2000) has no Mavor entry (printed p. 1255, where it would fall between 'Maurice, Dr Oliver' and 'Max'). Age on oath, for context only: Wilde, cross-examined in April 1895 about Taylor's rooms, put Mavor at 'About twenty-five or twenty-six', which would place his birth about 1869-70 and sits awkwardly with the 1866 of the Find a Grave memorial; McKenna, Secret Life (2008), p. 328, has him 'twenty' when Taylor picked him up in late September 1892, which would mean about 1872.
